0.note: The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]
See how you translated the expression “the sons of Korah” in the superscription to Psalm 42. Alternate translation: [of the descendants of Korah] or [of the Korahites]

1.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and do that here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Listen carefully to me, all of you people who live in the world] or [Hear this, all peoples! Yes, listen, everyone who lives in the world]
The implied “you” in these imperatives is plural because the psalmist is addressing many people. So use plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

2.note: The psalmist is using **sons of a human** as a common expression of his culture to mean “ordinary people,” and he is using **sons of a man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “distinguished people.” If these phrases do not have those meanings in your language, you could use comparable expressions from your language that do have those meanings, or you could state the meanings plainly. Alternate translation: [both the man on the street and the man in the corner office] or [both ordinary people and distinguished people]

The psalmist is using the adjectives **rich** and **poor** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjective with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [rich people and poor people]

3.q: פִּ֭⁠י יְדַבֵּ֣ר חָכְמ֑וֹת וְ⁠הָג֖וּת לִבִּ֣⁠י תְבוּנֽוֹת
3.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [My mouth will speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart will speak understanding]

3.q: פִּ֭⁠י יְדַבֵּ֣ר חָכְמ֑וֹת וְ⁠הָג֖וּת לִבִּ֣⁠י תְבוּנֽוֹת
3.note: The psalmist is using individual parts of a himself, his **mouth** and the **meditation of his heart**, to mean all of him in the act of speaking **wisdom** and **understanding**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [With my mouth I will speak wisdom, and from the meditation of my heart I will speak understanding]

Here the **heart** represents a person’s thoughts. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and from the meditation of my thoughts I will speak understanding]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **meditation** and **understanding**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [and from what I have meditated on in my thoughts, I will say things that will help you understand]

4.note: The psalmist is speaking as if he is going to physically **incline** his **ear**, that is, lean over the way someone would do to listen to someone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will listen carefully to a proverb]

The psalmist is speaking of this **proverb** as if it were a living thing that could speak to him. While he actually could listen to this proverb in the sense of hearing other people quote it, he means that he will carefully consider its meaning. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [I will see what a proverb has to say to me] or [I will carefully consider the meaning of a proverb]

While the term that the ULT translates as **proverb** generally means a short, popular saying that expresses some wisdom or truth, the specific meaning in this context is a “comparison,” which many proverbs draw. The psalmist is probably referring to the comparison in the refrain in verses 12 and 20 of this psalm, that people are like beasts. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I will carefully consider the meaning of a comparison]

The psalmist is speaking as if his **enigma** (the difficult and puzzling question he is trying to solve) were a closed container that he is going to use a **harp** to **open**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will explain my enigma as I sing and accompany myself with a harp]

5.q: לָ֣⁠מָּה אִ֭ירָא בִּ֣⁠ימֵי רָ֑ע עֲוֺ֖ן עֲקֵבַ֣⁠י יְסוּבֵּֽ⁠נִי׃ הַ⁠בֹּטְחִ֥ים עַל־חֵילָ֑⁠ם וּ⁠בְ⁠רֹ֥ב עָ֝שְׁרָ֗⁠ם יִתְהַלָּֽלוּ
5.note: If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine 49:5 and 49:6 into a verse bridge in order to keep together the entire question that the psalmist is asking in these verses. The psalmist is using the question form to make a confident affirmation. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I do not have to be afraid in the days of evil, when the iniquity of my heels surrounds me, the ones trusting in their wealth, and in the abundance of their treasure they boast!]

The psalmist is using the term **days** to mean “time,” since time consists of days. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [during evil times] or [during troubled times]

As the next verse indicates, the psalmist is using his **heels** to represent people who would trip him up at his heels, that is, make him fall down. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [when the iniquity of those who would trip me up surrounds me]

The psalmist is speaking as if people wanted to trip him physically and make him fall down. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [when the iniquity of those who want to cause my downfall surrounds me] or [when the iniquity of those who want to ruin me surrounds me]

The psalmist is speaking of the **iniquity** of certain people as if it were a living thing that could surround him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when iniquitous people who want to ruin me surround me]

6.note: The psalmist is using two different verb forms in parallel statements. It may be more natural in your language to use the same verb form in both statements. Alternate translation: [the ones trusting in their wealth and boasting in the abundance of their treasure]

7.q: אָ֗ח לֹא־פָדֹ֣ה יִפְדֶּ֣ה אִ֑ישׁ לֹא־יִתֵּ֖ן לֵ⁠אלֹהִ֣ים כָּפְרֽ⁠וֹ
7.note: The psalmist is repeating forms of the verb **redeem** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [A man certainly does not redeem a brother, he does not give his ransom to God]

7.q: אָ֗ח לֹא־פָדֹ֣ה יִפְדֶּ֣ה אִ֑ישׁ לֹא־יִתֵּ֖ן לֵ⁠אלֹהִ֣ים כָּפְרֽ⁠וֹ
7.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [A man certainly does not pay a ransom to God to redeem a brother]

The psalmist is speaking as if a fellow human being were actually another person’s **brother**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a fellow human]

8.q: וְ֭⁠יֵקַר פִּדְי֥וֹן נַפְשָׁ֗⁠ם וְ⁠חָדַ֥ל לְ⁠עוֹלָֽם׃ וִֽ⁠יחִי־ע֥וֹד לָ⁠נֶ֑צַח לֹ֖א יִרְאֶ֣ה הַ⁠שָּֽׁחַת
8.note: If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine verses 8 and 9 into a verse bridge in order to put the information about what **the redemption of their life** means right after that phrase. Alternate translation: [For the redemption of their life, that one should live on forever, that one should not see the pit, is costly, and it ceases forever]

In this verse, the word **life** is singular in form, but it refers to the lives of all humans as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “life.” Alternate translation: [their lives]

The psalmist means that the attempt at the **redemption** of a life **ceases** in the sense that it does not succeed and must be abandoned. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and the attempt always fails]

9.note: In this context, the term **see** has the sense of “experience.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [that one should not experience the pit]

The psalmist is using the expression **the pit** to refer to Sheol, the realm of the dead. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [that one should not experience the grave] or [that one should not go to the realm of the dead]

10.note: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [After all,]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [one will see the Pit]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wise** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [Wise people]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **fool** or **brute**. He means such people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [fools and brutes] or [foolish people and brutish people]

11.note: This phrase is a translation of the written Hebrew text. You may wish to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation. Alternate translation: [Their graves {are} their houses forever]

Here, what is **Inside** people represents their thoughts. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [In their thoughts]

The psalmist is using a common expression of his culture to mean that the people he is describing give new names, their own names, to **lands** or properties. If this expression does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They give their names to lands] or [They name lands after themselves]

12.note: The expressions **is likened** and **are destroyed** are passive verbal forms. If your language would not use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [He is like the beasts, which perish]

13.note: In this context, **to them** is a possessive form. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [This, their way, is their folly]

The psalmist is speaking of how people live as if that were a **way** or path that they were walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [This, their manner of life, is their folly]

The psalmist is speaking as if those who admire them and want to be like these presumptuous rich people were walking **after** them on the same **way** or path. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [but their followers delight]

The psalmist is using the **mouths** of these presumptuous rich people to represent what they say by using their mouths. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in their sayings]
To translate the term **Selah** here and in verse 15, see how your translation team decided to represent that term in 3:2.

14.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **sheep** are vulnerable and easily killed, so these rich people are vulnerable to dying. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [As if they were vulnerable sheep]

Here the psalmist is using the pronoun **They** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. If you need to say specifically who does the action, the context in the next verse indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [They are appointed] or [God appoints them]

The psalmist is speaking of **death** as if it were a living thing that could **shepherd** these people. He means that just as a shepherd keeps all of his sheep under his control so that none wander away, none of these people will get away from the realm of the dead. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. (However, since the image of a **shepherd** here extends the image of **sheep** earlier in the verse, you may wish to express both images as comparisons. The UST models one way to do that.) Alternate translation: [they will not get away from the realm of the dead]

The psalmist is speaking as if the **upright** were going to rule **in the morning** on a certain day over rich people who had been wicked. He means that the “days of evil” (that is, the troubled times) that he began describing in verse 5, pictured here as a dark night, will surely end as God delivers innocent people from oppression. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar expression in 46:5. Alternate translation: [And when God delivers the upright from their oppression, they will rule over them]

The psalmist is using the adjective **upright** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [upright people]

The psalmist is speaking of **Sheol** as if it were a living thing that could **consume** the **form** or body of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and their body will decompose in the grave]

In this verse, the word **form** is singular in form, but it refers to the forms or bodies of these wicked people as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “form.” Alternate translation: [their forms] or [their bodies]
The pronoun **it** refers to the **form** of each wicked person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [from its dwelling] or [away from where they lived]

15.note: Here, **hand** represents the power and control that a person or thing has over someone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the control of Sheol] or [from the custody of Sheol]

Here the word **for** introduces not a reason but an explanation. Use a connecting word or phrase in your language that will show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [and he will do that by taking me]

16.note: Here the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [a person]

Here, a rich person’s **house** represents all of his possessions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [when the splendor of his estate increases]

17.note: Here, **glory** represents “wealth.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [his wealth]

The psalmist assumes that readers will understand that by **go down**, he means “go down to Sheol.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [go down to Sheol]

18.note: The psalmist is using one part of a person, his **soul**, to mean all of him in the act of blessing himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he blesses himself]

While the term “bless” usually refers to expressing hope that good things would happen to a person, in this context, it means saying that good things have happened to a person. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [he congratulates himself]

Here the psalmist is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and people do praise you when you do well for yourself] or [and you are praised when you do well for yourself]

The words **you** and **yourself** are singular here because the psalmist is addressing each person in the audience as a representative individual who needs to consider whether what he says applies directly to him. So use singular forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction. If it does not, you may be able to communicate the meaning here in some other way. Alternate translation: [and they will praise any one of you if you do well for yourself] or [and any one of you will be praised if he does well for himself]

19.note: In a context such as this, your language might say “go” instead of **come**. Alternate translation: [he will go to the generation of his fathers]

The psalmist is using the term **fathers** to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will come to the generation of his ancestors]

The psalmist assumes that his listeners will understand that by this phrase he means that the rich man he has been describing since verse 16 will join in death the **generation** of people that consists of his ancestors. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [he will join his ancestors in death]

The psalmist is using **they will not see light** as a common expression of his culture to mean that the rich man and his ancestors will not live on the earth again. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they will never see the light of day] or [they will never live on the earth again]

20.q: אָדָ֣ם בִּ֭⁠יקָר וְ⁠לֹ֣א יָבִ֑ין נִמְשַׁ֖ל כַּ⁠בְּהֵמ֣וֹת
20.note: **A human in honor, but he does not understand** introduces the first part of a possible condition. What the psalmist describes in the rest of this verse is true if this condition happens. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [Suppose a human is in honor, but he does not understand. Then he is likened to the beasts]

This is the second occurrence of the refrain in this psalm. We recommend that you show this to your readers by translating the phrases here the same way that you translated them in the first occurrence of this refrain in 49:12. Alternate translation: [he is like the beasts, which perish]
